---
title: "016 — GitHub Copilot support"
---

> **Status:** standing (the four manual smokes needing a real Copilot subscription
> remain logged for user validation, as with 007's real-key chats)

**Goal.** Make Mayon usable on the requester's workplace main AI: GitHub Copilot as a
first-class provider kind. Add it in settings, authorize with a GitHub account through
the device flow without ever copying a secret, and chat with streamed replies and tool
calls at full parity with any other provider. Renewal of short-lived access is
invisible; a dead grant surfaces a provider-specific reconnect state with one action;
the model list comes live from the account's catalog with a curated fallback; multiple
accounts coexist. The bar: add-to-first-reply in under three minutes with zero manual
secret handling, and 100% of expiry-affected requests completing without user
interaction.

**Why.** A standalone spec — no idea deck; a direct user need ("that's our main AI in
my official work") following the provider-template features 007/008, and the first case
that broke the template pattern: templates can only serve a pasted static key, and the
whole point here was account authorization with renewable, short-lived access — the PAT
path was rejected by construction. Research was done with measured CORS probes rather
than documentation: github.com's device-flow endpoints send no CORS headers at all,
while the Copilot API answers browser calls with permissive CORS — an undocumented
accident.

**Outcome & reversals.** Specced and implemented August 29, merged September 2 after
two review rounds (PRs #11 and #13). Topology: the device flow runs server-side (flow
state in memory, the device code never leaves), the resulting GitHub grant lives in the
browser KeyStore under the provider id — the constitution's one secret home — and the
server mints short-lived Copilot session tokens with 120-second eager refresh and
single-flight caching. Serving reuses `createOpenAICompatible` behind a session-aware
fetch injecting the mandatory header set (measured: 400 without the integration id, 403
without editor headers), targeting the endpoint the exchange declares authoritative, so
Business/Enterprise hosts come free. Renewal, revocation, and quota map onto typed
errors — auth-required, subscription-required, and the existing rate limit carrying
`Retry-After` — so the chat store never learns a new kind. Discovery filters to
chat-capable, policy-enabled models and deliberately ignores `model_picker_enabled`, a
known source of false negatives. Zero schema changes; the provider catalog grew 17→18
with order tests extended. Two alternatives were rejected outright: browser-direct
exchange (it would pin the feature to undocumented CORS) and server-side grant storage
(the KeyStore rule exists precisely to avoid server-held user credentials). The
accepted risk is recorded, not hidden: the Copilot API surface and the
ecosystem-standard client id are undocumented and ToS-gray, so both sit in one
constants module — a future official path is a one-file change. The server API contract
is preserved verbatim at
[appendices/016-copilot-server-api.md](appendices/016-copilot-server-api.md).

**Learnings.**

- Provider kind, not template, is the unit of customization when auth — not wire
  format — is what differs.
- Probe CORS empirically before choosing auth topology; a permissive header today is
  not a contract.
- Map the observable failure families (expiry, revocation, quota) onto typed errors and
  upstream quirks never reach the chat store.
- Isolate ToS-gray constants in one module so the risk is a one-file swap, not a
  rewrite.
- Even server-required features must define their server-absent degradation path.
